newsitem.title: INDIA: India's planning body aims at 7 pct annual growth.
newsitem.headline: India's planning body aims at 7 pct annual growth.

text.p: India's Planning Commission said on Thursday it was targeting an accelerated seven percent annual economic growth rate for the country's ninth five-year plan beginning on April 1, 1997.
"We have projected a growth rate of seven percent and it is sustainable," commission Deputy Chairman Madhu Dandavate told reporters.

He said the growth rate, which was targeted at 5.9 percent in the eighth plan (1992-1997), would be stepped up by stimulating the savings rate and the efficient use of the funds invested in the economy.
"We have not exaggerated the growth rate at all," he said.
Dandavate said the draft approach paper for the ninth plan had been unanimously endorsed and accepted by Prime Minister H. D. Deve Gowda's cabinet earlier this week.
He said the National Development Council, which includes all the chief ministers, would meet on January 16 to endorse the document.
Dandavate said detailed work on the plan would begin after finding out the resources of the states at a meeting of chief ministers on January 4.

He said the paper envisaged a total plan outlay of 8,750 billion rupees in 1997-2002, compared with 6,310 billion rupees in the previous plan. This would include a capital investment of 7,600 billion rupees and current outlay of 1,150 billion rupees.
The Planning Commission has also set a 9.3 percent annual growth target for industrial growth and more than 4.5 percent agricultural growth for the next five years.
The paper set a current account deficit of 2.4 percent of GDP in the ninth plan, compared with 1.3 percent in the previous period, and a fiscal deficit of four percent of GDP in the ninth plan.
The target for annual export growth was set at 14.5 percent for the 1997-2002 period, compared with 11.4 percent in the previous five-year plan.
Annual import growth was targeted at 15.3 percent, compared with 13.6 percent in the previous plan.
Dandavate said the higher import target was due to projected increases in essential imports like petroleum and in order to modernise industry.

Dandavate said the incremental capital output ratio (ICOR), which measures the number of units of capital required to produce one unit of output, was expected to come down to 4.08 in the ninth plan from 4.24 in the present one.
A lower ICOR indicates higher economic efficiency.
The government was looking for a domestic savings rate of 26.2 percent in the ninth plan, down from 23.7 percent in the current plan, he said.
"Our thrust will be to give impetus to savings when the budget is presented by the finance minister (in February)," Dandavate said.
Dandavate said the commission favoured greater compliance of taxes and felt the taxation structure itself fell within the ambit of the finance ministry.
"We are aiming at growth with equity, growth with distributive justice and growth with social justice," he said.

Listing the objectives of the ninth plan, Dandavate said priority would be given to agriculture and rural development to generate employment, to accelerate the rate of growth of the economy through stable prices and to contain population growth.
"A social and human base will be emphasised in the plan," he said.
